[00:00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. Ethan my SE is here too. Quick intro?
[00:00:12] Nina Shah: Nina, head of ML at Crescent Bank. Carlos from platform and Aisha infra. Tom in procurement.
[00:00:25] Maya: Great. Agenda today is Optimize walkthrough — batching and prefix/KV cache, and a simple cost model so you can see tradeoffs. We'll do Q&A as we go.
[00:00:40] Ethan Wu: I'll start with the high-level: two levers we usually pull are batching and caching. Batching improves GPU throughput but can increase tail latency; caching (prefix / KV) reduces token compute for repeated context.
[00:01:05] Carlos Mendes: Quick Q — when you say prefix cache, is that the same thing as the KV cache folks mention? I'm mixing terms.
[00:01:12] Ethan: Good question — slight nuance: prefix cache is caching decoded embeddings for initial prompt prefixes, whereas KV cache is the key/value attention state for previously computed tokens. In practice Redwood supports both patterns; sometimes customers call both "KV cache" and we see mixed terminology in logs.
[00:01:35] Speaker 1: ...
[00:01:50] Maya: We'll show a cost model with numbers — rough ballpark — then we can plug in your traffic later.
[00:02:10] Ethan: Slide: baseline no-cache, low batching. Example: at 1 RPS with 20-token responses average, per-token cost is X, throughput very low. If we increase batch size to 8, you get ~3-4x token/sec improvement on GPU due to better utilization, but p95 latency can jump from 120ms to 320ms if you wait for batch assembly.
[00:03:05] Nina: Our SLO is p95 below 300ms for customer-facing flows — latency is strict.
[00:03:12] Ethan: Right. That's why we recommend dynamic batching: start sending smaller immediate batches and then opportunistically batch during spikes. Redwood's runtime supports a latency-aware scheduler — you can set a latency target and it will balance batching.
[00:03:33] Aisha Rahman: Do you have numbers for throughput vs latency with the scheduler?
[00:03:38] Ethan: Example from a fintech customer: at target p95 250ms we got ~2.6x throughput uplift vs naive per-request inference; with p95 relaxed to 500ms we hit 5x. These are workload-dependent, of course.
[00:04:02] Carlos: And caching? How do hit rates map to cost savings?
[00:04:07] Ethan: With a prefix/KV cache, cost savings are roughly proportional to the cache hit-rate times average token compute per cached prefix. If you have a 70% prefix reuse rate for static prompts, you can cut token compute by ~60% depending on how many tokens the prefix accounts for. We typically model three components: cold path (miss — full compute), warm path (partial hit), and hot path (full hit — e.g., only final generation needed).
[00:04:40] Maya: I'll type a simple formula in the notes: total_tokens_compute = total_requests * avg_response_tokens * (1 - hit_rate) + caching_overhead. For cost model we convert compute to GPU-seconds and then to $ by node-hour.
[00:04:58] Tom Ellis: Is the cache state stored in the control plane? Any PII concerns?
[00:05:05] Ethan: Good point. For Hosted we store cache metadata encrypted; you can opt out of prefix caching for sensitive prompts. For Dedicated and Private (VPC/on-prem) the cache stores run in your network and can be backed by your KMS/HSM — so you retain control. We'll share the security notes.
[00:05:30] Nina: We will require SOC2 + audit logs for any hosted caches.
[00:05:35] Maya: Understood — we'll send SOC2 docs and audit log details.
[00:05:50] Ethan: Back to batching: there's also continuous batching for streaming calls — we do partial response streaming while still batching subsequent tokens, so you don't have to sacrifice UX.
[00:06:18] Carlos: Do you support KV cache invalidation when models update or when rolling out a new tokenizer?
[00:06:25] Ethan: Yes, cache invalidation policies are versioned with model pinning. When you rollout a model variant we create a new cache namespace; you can also provide TTLs or do manual invalidation. Best practice: pin serving model per rollout and warm cache with a pre-warm job.
[00:06:50] Speaker 2: [crosstalk] 
[00:07:05] Ethan: Now I'll show the micro benchmark we typically run: we replay a sample traffic histogram, measure token/sec and p95 under different batch sizes and hit rates.
[00:07:22] Ethan: Example numbers (toy model): batch=1 -> 120 tokens/sec, p95 110ms; batch=8 -> 380 tokens/sec, p95 320ms; batch=16 -> 520 tokens/sec, p95 420ms. With KV cache hit 50% those token/sec numbers effectively double in cost-effectiveness.
[00:07:50] Nina: For our chat assistant, many prompts share a long policy prefix — sounds like a good candidate for prefix caching.
[00:07:58] Aisha: How much memory does KV cache require? That impacts node sizing.
[00:08:03] Ethan: KV cache size depends on sequence length and number of cached contexts. Example: a 2k token context KV for a 32K model is ~X MB per context — sorry that number varies, I don't want to misstate; we'll share a sizing sheet. In practice we compute cache budget: expected unique contexts * per-context KV size + overhead.
[00:08:30] Carlos: If we pre-warm cache, how long until hit-rate stabilizes?
[00:08:35] Ethan: Depends on traffic locality. For a small set of repeated flows, hours; for broader sessions maybe days. We often see 60-80% stable hit for templated prompts within 24 hours if you pre-warm with top N prefixes.
[00:08:55] Maya: Quick pause — we've got the high-level tradeoffs. Any blockers from procurement or security?
[00:09:03] Tom Ellis: Procurement mostly needs pricing and an outline of SLA. If Dedicated monthly commit, what does typical price look like?
[00:09:12] Maya: We'll send a sample Dedicated proposal. For a rough sense the Dedicated pools are priced by committed GPU-hours plus a platform fee; the per-token will be much lower than hosted at scale because of utilization. We'll attach a worked example in the proposal.
[00:09:35] Ethan: Returning to cost model: here's a quick worked example we typed live — assume 100k requests/day, avg 50 tokens generated, 30% cache hit. That yields N tokens compute/day -> convert to nominal GPU-hours -> $Y/day. If you increase cache hit to 60% you cut compute by ~30-35% in tokens.
[00:10:05] Nina: Can Redwood provide the bench harness so we can run it in our lab?
[00:10:10] Ethan: Yes — we'll share the bench script and a Jupyter that replays your traffic. It does per-request timing, batch occupancy, and effective p99/p95.
[00:10:25] Carlos: Any special instrumentation we should output to measure hit-rate?
[00:10:30] Ethan: Emit per-request metadata: prompt-id or prefix-hash (hashed in prod), response tokens, cache_hit boolean, and batch_size. That will let us compute effective savings.

[00:11:20] Maya: Let's go through a couple of scenarios: 1) Low-latency customer-facing chat (p95 < 300ms) — we bias towards smaller batch sizes + aggressive pre-warming for critical prefixes; 2) Batch background generation (reporting) — we favor large batch sizes and high throughput; 3) Mixed workloads — we route by policy (latency vs cost).
[00:11:55] Nina: For mixed, can Redwood route in the same pool? We want to avoid separate infra for separate tiers.
[00:12:02] Ethan: Yes — routing policies can send requests to different queues with SLO-aware schedulers; Redwood can also expose cost-center tagging and per-route dashboards.
[00:12:22] Carlos: About prefix privacy: if a prefix includes PHI we must not store it. How granular is control?
[00:12:29] Ethan: You can mark prefixes as non-cacheable at request time. Also with Private deployment the cache lives in your VPC and you control encryption keys. We'll share the policy doc.

[00:14:12] Carlos: Does pre-warm cost compute? Does it show up in billing?
[00:14:17] Ethan: Yes it consumes compute and is billed like any inference run; you can subtract that one-time cost when you compare ongoing savings.

[00:15:45] Maya: I'll run a quick example with your numbers if you can share token distribution. Carlos?

[00:16:05] Ethan: For KV cache eviction policies we recommend LRU with periodic TTLs for ephemeral contexts. For financial templates you can set longer TTLs.
[00:16:25] Nina: How does model quantization affect caching or batching?
[00:16:30] Ethan: Quantization impacts GPU memory and throughput; smaller models or quantized kernels reduce per-token compute and allow higher batch sizes before hitting memory limits. Cache semantics stay the same but per-context KV size can change slightly.
[00:16:55] Aisha: Any constraints on tokenizer mismatch when warming cache across model variants?
[00:17:00] Ethan: You should only reuse caches across variants with identical tokenization; we enforce namespace separation otherwise.

[00:18:40] Ethan: Yes on Private deployment we offer a bring-your-own-license or on-prem package; for Dedicated we can spin up a test pool in your VPC with customer routing. We'll follow up with options.
